Empirical Research Plan  
“Education, Health, and the Mechanisms Linking Them”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS) difference-in-differences design.

• Idea:  Use exogenous variation in years of schooling generated by changes in state-level compulsory-schooling laws (CSLs) that raised the minimum school-leaving age or the number of required grades.  
• Execution:  Code each individual’s potential exposure to the CSL in the state in which she was born.  Compare adjacent birth cohorts within the same state, before vs. after the law rose.  This is effectively a stacked DID whose interaction (state × post-law) is used as an instrument for schooling.

Why appropriate?  
– The NHIS provides birthplace, year of birth, and education; CSLs vary sharply across state and cohort and have been widely validated as strong predictors of schooling.  
– Health is observed long after schooling is completed, so reverse causality (early health affecting attained schooling) is mitigated.  
– Because the same policy shock is used for thousands of individuals, the first stage is strong and the LATE is well-defined.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (“dose”):  Years of completed schooling (continuous) or indicators such as High-school graduate = 1.

Instrument (= first-stage treatment):  
Zist  = 1 if individual i born in state s and cohort t turned the pre-law leaving age after the new CSL became binding; 0 otherwise.

Control / counterfactual:  Cohorts in the same state born just before the CSL change (and thus not bound by the higher requirement).

Timing:  Each state-specific effective date of the CSL.  Our sample window (birth cohorts 1920–1975) covers scores of discrete reforms.

No running variable is necessary for canonical 2SLS, but in robustness we will implement a fuzzy RDD that uses year-of-birth distance to the state-specific cutoff as the running variable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1  Relevance:  CSL exposure significantly raises completed schooling.  
 – Extensive evidence from prior work; will verify F-stats > 10 in first stage.

A2  Exclusion:  CSL reforms affect adult health only through their impact on schooling, not through other policy channels.  
 – Plausible because CSLs target school-leaving age; most coincident child-labor laws pre-date our reforms.  Still, will include state-of-birth × year-of-birth quadratic trends and controls for contemporaneous child-labor index.

A3  Parallel cohort trends within state (DID component):  In absence of the law, adjacent cohorts would have exhibited parallel trends in health.  
 – Reasonable over narrow cohort windows (±5 years).  Checked with event-study plot of reduced-form health gaps.

A4  No selective migration around birth:  Families did not sort into states in anticipation of future CSL changes (hard because CSLs are legislated after most sample parents have already located).  
 – We use state of birth, not state of residence, and restrict to respondents whose parents were native to that state in robustness.

A5  Monotonicity (IV):  Everyone exposed to a stricter CSL weakly increases schooling; no “defiers.”  
 – Believable because the reform legally forbids early exit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1:  Other state-level educational or health policies change at the same time.  
Mitigation:  Add controls for 1950–1980 state public-health spending, Medicaid adoption year, and state-specific linear birth-cohort trends.

Threat 2:  Differential mortality before the NHIS interview (cohort survival bias).  
Mitigation:  Limit sample to cohorts ≤ 65 at interview; replicate results using self-reported childhood health (available in 2000 NHIS) as a control.

Threat 3:  Measurement error in CSL coding or in state-of-birth.  
Mitigation:  Cross-check CSL dates with Goldin-Katz series; run sensitivity deleting states with ambiguous legislation; cluster SEs by state of birth.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------- Libraries --------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast felm / iv
library(haven)       # read dta/sas if needed
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# -------------------- Load Data --------------------
nhis  <- read_csv("nhis_90_91_00.csv")      # pooled adult files
csl   <- read_csv("state_csl_birthcohort.csv") # state, cohort, CSL indicator

# -------------------- Prepare Variables ------------
analytic <- nhis %>%
  mutate(yob        = year - age,
         statebirth = fct_lump(state_birth, 50),
         edu_years  = ifelse(educ %in% 31:40, educ-30, NA), # example recode
         hsgrad     = as.integer(edu_years >= 12),
         race_black = (race == "Black"),
         female     = (sex == "Female")) %>%
  left_join(csl, by = c("statebirth" = "state", "yob" = "birthcohort")) %>%
  mutate(instrument = exposed_csl)

# Outcome examples
analytic <- analytic %>%
  mutate(mort5     = death_within5yr,          # from NDI linked file (1990 wave)
         smoke     = (smoking_status == "Current"),
         selfpoor  = (self_rated_health %in% c("Fair","Poor")))

# -------------------- 2SLS Main Spec ----------------
# Health = β * schooling + γX + δ_state + δ_cohort + ε
formula_iv <- mort5 ~ edu_years  | instrument ~ 0 +
              race_black + female + age + I(age^2) |
              statebirth + yob

mod_iv <- feols(formula_iv, data = analytic, cluster = ~statebirth)
summary(mod_iv)

# -------------------- First-Stage F -----------------
wald_iv(mod_iv, stage = 1)

# ---------------- Robustness:  ±5-year Window ------
analytic_narrow <- analytic %>% 
  group_by(statebirth) %>% 
  filter(abs(yob - csl_year) <= 5) %>% ungroup()

mod_iv_narrow <- feols(formula_iv, data = analytic_narrow, cluster = ~statebirth)
summary(mod_iv_narrow)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts a negative coefficient on mortality and adverse health events: extra schooling improves health.

Magnitude priors (based on prior US evidence):  
– One additional year of schooling lowers 5-year mortality by ≈ 0.1 pp (i.e., from 2.5% to 2.4%).  
– Reduces current smoking prevalence by 2–3 pp; lowers probability of self-rated fair/poor health by about 1 pp.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1  Relevance (first-stage F > 10):            1  
C2  Exclusion (no other channels):             0.5  
C3  Parallel trends / cohort comparability:    0.8  
C4  No selective migration / composition:      0.7  
C5  SUTVA / no spillovers across states:       0.9  

Overall the design is credible but, as always with CSL instruments, exclusion and migration assumptions deserve careful scrutiny and extensive robustness work.
